title: Ἑλένη τοὺς Ἀχαιοὺς ὀνομάζει
about: Helen answers Priam’s question: the huge man is Agamemnon, her husband’s brother. Priam calls him fortunate, remembers the Phrygians and Amazons he once saw, and says the Achaeans were more numerous. Asked about the next man, Helen names Odysseus, and Antenor tells how Odysseus and Menelaus spoke before the Trojans: Menelaus clear and brief, Odysseus standing stiff and looking down until his voice came out like snowflakes. Asked about the third, Helen names Ajax and Idomeneus, and says she cannot see her own brothers Castor and Polydeuces; the poet adds that the earth already held them in Lacedaemon. Heralds carry the lambs and wine through the city, and Idaeus calls Priam to the plain to swear the oaths for the duel over Helen. Priam shudders, has the horses yoked, mounts the chariot with Antenor, and they drive out through the Scaean Gates.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ Ἑλένη μύθοισιν ἀμείβετο δῖα γυναικῶν·
sentences.l: Him then Helen with words answered, heavenly-one of women:
sentences.i: Then Helen, heavenly among women, answered him with words:
sentences.n: τὸν δ’ … ἀμείβετο is the reply formula: τὸν ‘him’ is Priam, whose speech has just ended, and ἀμείβετο is the imperfect of ἀμείβομαι ‘answer’, here with μύθοισιν ‘with words’ (the epic dative plural of μῦθος). δῖα γυναικῶν is a stock phrase, ‘heavenly-one of women’ (δῖα being the feminine of δῖος ‘heavenly’), translated the same way every time.

sentences.t: αἰδοῖός τέ μοί ἐσσι φίλε ἑκυρὲ δεινός τε·
sentences.l: “Revered to me you are, dear father-in-law, and dread;
sentences.i: “To me you are revered, dear father-in-law, and dread;
sentences.n: αἰδοῖος is ‘worthy of reverence’ (house rendering ‘revered’) and δεινός ‘dread’, one who inspires awe (house rendering ‘dread’); τέ … τε joins them, and μοί ‘to me’ says whose feeling it is. ἐσσί is the epic second person of εἰμί ‘you are’, φίλε is the vocative of φίλος ‘dear’, and ἑκυρέ the vocative of ἑκυρός ‘husband’s father’: Helen is addressing Priam, the father of Alexander, and answering the kindness of 164–165. The line is metrically irregular as transmitted: it comes out as a hexameter only if the short last syllable of φίλε is counted long in the fourth foot and the short last syllable of ἑκυρέ is counted long before δεινός in the fifth (an older initial δϝ- is assumed), which leaves a spondee in the fifth foot.

sentences.t:
ὡς ὄφελεν θάνατός μοι ἁδεῖν κακὸς ὁππότε δεῦρο
υἱέϊ σῷ ἑπόμην θάλαμον γνωτούς τε λιποῦσα
παῖδά τε τηλυγέτην καὶ ὁμηλικίην ἐρατεινήν.
sentences.l:
Would that evil death had been pleasing to me, when hither
your son I followed, my chamber and kinsfolk leaving behind
and my child, late-born, and the company of my own age, lovely.
sentences.i: I wish that an evil death had pleased me on the day I followed your son here, leaving my chamber and my kinsfolk and my late-born child and the lovely company of my own age.
sentences.n: ὡς ὄφελεν … ἁδεῖν is a wish that was not fulfilled: ὄφελεν (the aorist of ὀφείλω, ‘ought’) with the aorist infinitive ἁδεῖν of ἁνδάνω ‘please’ and the dative μοι, so ‘would that death had pleased me’. ὁππότε is ‘when’, ἑπόμην the imperfect of ἕπομαι ‘follow’ with the dative υἱέϊ σῷ ‘your son’, and λιποῦσα the aorist participle (feminine, Helen) of λείπω ‘leaving’, with four objects: θάλαμον ‘chamber’, γνωτούς ‘kinsfolk’ (blood relations), παῖδα ‘child’ and ὁμηλικίην (explained below). τηλύγετος is shipped in the Odyssey as ‘late-born’; the origin of the word is not known, so that is a traditional guess. ὁμηλικίη is ‘those of the same age’, her girlhood companions, and ἐρατεινός ‘lovely’.

sentences.t: ἀλλὰ τά γ’ οὐκ ἐγένοντο·
sentences.l: But those things did not come to pass;
sentences.i: But that did not come to pass;
sentences.n: τά γε is ‘those things at least’, the wish of 173–175, and ἐγένοντο is the aorist of γίγνομαι ‘came to be’. The ano teleia ends the clause, and the next words give the result.

sentences.t: τὸ καὶ κλαίουσα τέτηκα.
sentences.l: on that account, too, weeping, I have melted away.
sentences.i: and that is why I waste away in tears.
sentences.n: τό is ‘on that account’, a neuter pronoun used as an adverb, with καί ‘also, even’. κλαίουσα is the feminine participle of κλαίω ‘weep’ (Helen), and τέτηκα the perfect of τήκω ‘melt’, which in the perfect is intransitive: ‘I have melted, wasted away’.

sentences.t: τοῦτο δέ τοι ἐρέω ὅ μ’ ἀνείρεαι ἠδὲ μεταλλᾷς·
sentences.l: but this to you I will tell, which me you ask and inquire after:
sentences.i: But this I will tell you, what you ask me and inquire after:
sentences.n: The line also stands in the Odyssey, and is given the same English, with a colon now because the answer follows. τοι is σοι ‘to you’ (enclitic), ἐρέω the future ‘I will say’, ὅ the relative ‘what’, ἀνείρεαι the second-person middle of ἀνείρομαι ‘ask’, and μεταλλᾷς the contracted present of μεταλλάω ‘inquire after’. She is answering the question of 166–167.

sentences.t:
οὗτός γ’ Ἀτρεΐδης εὐρὺ κρείων Ἀγαμέμνων,
ἀμφότερον βασιλεύς τ’ ἀγαθὸς κρατερός τ’ αἰχμητής·
sentences.l:
This one indeed is Atreus’-son, wide-ruling Agamemnon,
both a king, a good one, and a strong spearman;
sentences.i: This is the son of Atreus, wide-ruling Agamemnon, both a good king and a strong spearman;
sentences.n: οὗτος γε is ‘this one’, pointing him out, and Ἀτρεΐδης is the patronymic ‘son of Atreus’. εὐρὺ κρείων (printed as two words) is ‘wide-ruling’ (the adverb εὐρύ ‘widely’ with κρείων ‘ruling’), a stock epithet of Agamemnon, translated the same way every time. ἀμφότερον is a neuter adverb, ‘in both ways’, answered by τε … τε. αἰχμητής is ‘spearman’, from αἰχμή ‘spear-point’; κρατερός is ‘strong’.

sentences.t: δαὴρ αὖτ’ ἐμὸς ἔσκε κυνώπιδος, εἴ ποτ’ ἔην γε.
sentences.l: husband’s-brother also he was, my own, of a dog-faced woman, if ever that was so.”
sentences.i: and he was my husband’s brother, too, shameless creature that I am, if ever that was so.”
sentences.n: δαήρ is ‘husband’s brother’: Agamemnon is the brother of Menelaus, Helen’s husband; αὖτ’ is ‘also, moreover’, and ἔσκε is an iterative form of εἰμί, here simply ‘was’. κυνώπιδος, ‘of a dog-faced woman’, is the genitive of κυνῶπις, Helen’s standing word of self-reproach (the Odyssey table renders it ‘dog-faced’ in the literal layer and ‘shameless’ in the English). εἴ ποτ’ ἔην γε, ‘if ever it was so’, is bitter: ἔην is ἦν, and she speaks as if the old tie were something long gone. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς φάτο, τὸν δ’ ὁ γέρων ἠγάσσατο φώνησέν τε·
sentences.l: So she spoke, and the old man was in wonder at him, and spoke:
sentences.i: So she spoke, and the old man was amazed at him and spoke:
sentences.n: ὣς φάτο is the speech-closing formula ‘so she spoke’ (φάτο is φημί unaugmented). ὁ γέρων is ‘the old man’, Priam, and τόν is Agamemnon, the object of ἠγάσσατο, the aorist of ἀγάομαι ‘be amazed at’ (the verb shipped as ‘in wonder’ / ‘were amazed at’; it comes again at 224). φώνησεν ‘spoke’ gets its accent from the enclitic τε.

sentences.t:
ὦ μάκαρ Ἀτρεΐδη μοιρηγενὲς ὀλβιόδαιμον,
ἦ ῥά νύ τοι πολλοὶ δεδμήατο κοῦροι Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.l:
“O blessed Atreus’-son, fate-born, prosperous in fortune,
truly now, to you many were subdued, the young men of the Achaeans.
sentences.i: “O blessed son of Atreus, born to your fate, prosperous in fortune, many young men of the Achaeans were indeed made subject to you.
sentences.n: ὦ μάκαρ … ὀλβιόδαιμον is a string of vocatives: μάκαρ ‘blessed’, μοιρηγενές ‘fate-born’, a compound of μοῖρα ‘portion, fate’ and a root meaning ‘born’ (the exact sense, ‘born to a destined lot’ or ‘born under a destiny’, is not known), and ὀλβιόδαιμον ‘prosperous in fortune’ (ὄλβιος ‘prosperous’ with δαίμων ‘lot, fortune’). ἦ ῥά νύ is ‘truly, then, now’. δεδμήατο is the epic third plural pluperfect passive of δάμνημι ‘subdue’ (literally ‘had been subdued’; the pluperfect states a past condition, so ‘were subdued’), with the dative τοι ‘to you’, the sense being that the Achaean youths are under Agamemnon’s power; κοῦροι ‘young men’.

sentences.t:
ἤδη καὶ Φρυγίην εἰσήλυθον ἀμπελόεσσαν,
ἔνθα ἴδον πλείστους Φρύγας ἀνέρας αἰολοπώλους
λαοὺς Ὀτρῆος καὶ Μυγδόνος ἀντιθέοιο,
οἵ ῥα τότ’ ἐστρατόωντο παρ’ ὄχθας Σαγγαρίοιο·
sentences.l:
Already I too went into Phrygia, vine-clad,
where I saw very many Phrygian men with gleaming colts,
the people of Otreus and of Mygdon, godlike,
who then were encamped along the banks of the Sangarius;
sentences.i: I too have been to vine-clad Phrygia, where I saw very many Phrygian men with their gleaming colts, the people of Otreus and of godlike Mygdon, who were then encamped along the banks of the Sangarius;
sentences.n: ἤδη καί is ‘already, once, too’, and εἰσήλυθον the aorist of εἰσέρχομαι ‘go into’. ἀμπελόεσσαν ‘vine-clad’ is the English already shipped for Epidaurus in the Catalogue. πλείστους is the superlative of πολύς, ‘very many’. αἰολοπώλους is a compound of αἰόλος and πῶλος ‘colt’; αἰόλος means ‘quick-moving’ or ‘gleaming’ or ‘dappled’, and which of these is meant is not known, so ‘gleaming colts’ is a choice. Ὀτρῆος and Μυγδόνος are genitives of the leaders’ names, ἀντιθέοιο ‘godlike’ the epic genitive of ἀντίθεος. ἐστρατόωντο is the imperfect of στρατάομαι ‘be encamped’, and ὄχθας ‘banks’ is the object of παρά ‘along’. Σαγγάριος is a river of Phrygia.

sentences.t:
καὶ γὰρ ἐγὼν ἐπίκουρος ἐὼν μετὰ τοῖσιν ἐλέχθην
ἤματι τῷ ὅτε τ’ ἦλθον Ἀμαζόνες ἀντιάνειραι·
sentences.l:
for I too, being an ally, was counted among them
on the day when the Amazons came, man-matching;
sentences.i: for I, as an ally, was numbered among them on the day the man-matching Amazons came;
sentences.n: καὶ γάρ is ‘for indeed’; ἐπίκουρος ἐών is ‘being an ally’, and ἐλέχθην the aorist passive of λέγω in its old sense ‘count, reckon’, so ‘I was counted’. ἤματι τῷ ὅτε τ’ is ‘on the day when’. Ἀμαζόνες ἀντιάνειραι: the epithet is ἀντί ‘against, equal to’ with ἀνήρ ‘man’, and whether it means ‘matching men’ or ‘fighting against men’ is disputed; ‘man-matching’ is kept to the first reading.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ οὐδ’ οἳ τόσοι ἦσαν ὅσοι ἑλίκωπες Ἀχαιοί.
sentences.l: but not even these were as many as the quick-eyed Achaeans.”
sentences.i: but even these were not so many as the quick-eyed Achaeans.”
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ οὐδ’ οἳ is ‘but not even they’, and τόσοι … ὅσοι ‘so many … as’. ἑλίκωπες Ἀχαιοί is ‘the quick-eyed Achaeans’, the epithet the Iliad table fixes; its sense is disputed. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: δεύτερον αὖτ’ Ὀδυσῆα ἰδὼν ἐρέειν’ ὁ γεραιός·
sentences.l: Second, in turn, seeing Odysseus, asked the old man:
sentences.i: Next, catching sight of Odysseus, the old man asked:
sentences.n: δεύτερον αὖτ’ is ‘second, in turn’, the second of the three Achaeans Priam asks about, and ἰδών the aorist participle ‘having seen’; ἐρέειν’ is ἐρέεινε, the imperfect of ἐρεείνω ‘ask’. ὁ γεραιός ‘the old man’ is Priam (see 181).

sentences.t: εἴπ’ ἄγε μοι καὶ τόνδε φίλον τέκος ὅς τις ὅδ’ ἐστί·
sentences.l: “Tell me, come, this one also, dear child, who this is;
sentences.i: “Come, dear child, tell me who this man is as well;
sentences.n: εἴπ’ is εἰπέ, the aorist imperative of ‘say’; ἄγε is the interjection ‘come’, and μοι ‘me’. καὶ τόνδε is ‘this one also’ (after Agamemnon), φίλον τέκος ‘dear child’ as at 162, and ὅς τις ὅδ’ ἐστί an indirect question, ‘who this one is’.

sentences.t:
μείων μὲν κεφαλῇ Ἀγαμέμνονος Ἀτρεΐδαο,
εὐρύτερος δ’ ὤμοισιν ἰδὲ στέρνοισιν ἰδέσθαι.
sentences.l:
Lesser by a head than Agamemnon, Atreus’-son,
but broader in the shoulders and in the chest to look at.
sentences.i: He is shorter by a head than Agamemnon, son of Atreus, but broader in the shoulders and chest to look at.
sentences.n: μείων is ‘smaller, less’, with κεφαλῇ ‘by a head’ (dative of measure) and the genitive Ἀγαμέμνονος for the comparison. εὐρύτερος is the comparative of εὐρύς ‘broad’, with ὤμοισιν ‘shoulders’ and στέρνοισιν ‘chest’ in the dative of respect; ἰδέσθαι is the aorist middle infinitive of ‘see’, ‘to look at’. Ἀτρεΐδαο is the epic genitive of the patronymic.

sentences.t:
τεύχεα μέν οἱ κεῖται ἐπὶ χθονὶ πουλυβοτείρῃ,
αὐτὸς δὲ κτίλος ὣς ἐπιπωλεῖται στίχας ἀνδρῶν·
sentences.l:
His armour lies upon the much-nourishing earth,
but he himself, like a tame ram, goes about the ranks of men;
sentences.i: His armour lies on the earth that feeds so many, but he himself ranges along the ranks of men like a tame ram;
sentences.n: τεύχεα is ‘armour’, and πουλυβοτείρῃ ‘much-nourishing’ is the stock epithet of the earth, rendered ‘that feeds so many’ in the English layer as in the shipped parts. αὐτός ‘he himself’ stands against the armour laid down. ἐπιπωλεῖται is ‘goes to and fro over’, with the accusative στίχας ‘ranks’. κτίλος is a word whose exact sense is not known: ‘tame’ is the usual guess, and the next line shows that a ram is meant, so ‘tame ram’ is read from the context.

sentences.t:
ἀρνειῷ μιν ἔγωγε ἐΐσκω πηγεσιμάλλῳ,
ὅς τ’ οἰῶν μέγα πῶϋ διέρχεται ἀργεννάων.
sentences.l:
I liken him, for my part, to a thick-fleeced ram,
which goes through the great flock of sheep, the white ones.”
sentences.i: I liken him to a thick-fleeced ram that goes through a great flock of white sheep.”
sentences.n: ἐΐσκω is ‘I liken’, with the dative ἀρνειῷ ‘to a ram’ and μιν ‘him’; ἔγωγε is ‘I for my part’. πηγεσιμάλλῳ is ‘thick-fleeced’ (πήγνυμι ‘make firm’ with μαλλός ‘fleece’). ὅς τ’ is ‘which’; οἰῶν is the genitive plural of ὄϊς ‘sheep’, πῶϋ ‘flock’, and ἀργεννάων the epic genitive plural of ἀργεννός ‘white’. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειθ’ Ἑλένη Διὸς ἐκγεγαυῖα·
sentences.l: Him then answered thereupon Helen, sprung of Zeus:
sentences.i: Then Helen, the daughter sprung from Zeus, answered him:
sentences.n: ἠμείβετ’ is ἠμείβετο ‘answered’, and ἔπειτα ‘then, thereupon’. Διὸς ἐκγεγαυῖα is the feminine perfect participle of ἐκγίγνομαι, ‘having sprung from Zeus’, Helen’s standing description (rendered ‘daughter sprung from Zeus’ at 4.184 in the Odyssey table).

sentences.t:
οὗτος δ’ αὖ Λαερτιάδης πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς,
ὃς τράφη ἐν δήμῳ Ἰθάκης κραναῆς περ ἐούσης
εἰδὼς παντοίους τε δόλους καὶ μήδεα πυκνά.
sentences.l:
“And this one in turn is Laertes’-son, many-wiled Odysseus,
who was reared in the land of Ithaca, rugged though it is,
knowing all kinds of tricks and solid counsels.”
sentences.i: “And this in turn is the son of Laertes, Odysseus of many wiles, who was reared in the land of Ithaca, rugged as it is, and knows all kinds of tricks and solid counsels.”
sentences.n: οὗτος … αὖ is ‘this one in turn’, and Λαερτιάδης the patronymic ‘son of Laertes’. πολύμητις is ‘many-wiled’ (house rendering ‘of many wiles’), the stock epithet. τράφη is ἐτράφη, the aorist passive of τρέφω ‘was reared’; δήμῳ is ‘land, district’, and κραναῆς περ ἐούσης ‘though it is rugged’ is the participle ἐούσης (= οὔσης) agreeing with Ἰθάκης, with περ ‘though’ (κραναός ‘rocky, rugged’). εἰδώς is the participle of οἶδα ‘knowing’, δόλους ‘tricks’, and μήδεα πυκνά ‘solid counsels’, the house rendering of πυκινὰ μήδεα. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ αὖτ’ Ἀντήνωρ πεπνυμένος ἀντίον ηὔδα·
sentences.l: To her in turn prudent Antenor spoke, face to face:
sentences.i: Then prudent Antenor spoke to her in turn, face to face:
sentences.n: τὴν δ’ αὖτ’ … ἀντίον ηὔδα is the reply formula with ‘in turn’ and ‘face to face’; ηὔδα is the imperfect of αὐδάω ‘speak’. πεπνυμένος ‘prudent’ is the stock epithet, translated the same way every time, as for Telemachus in the Odyssey.

sentences.t: ὦ γύναι ἦ μάλα τοῦτο ἔπος νημερτὲς ἔειπες·
sentences.l: “Woman, truly this word, unerring, you have spoken;
sentences.i: “Woman, the word you have spoken is truly unerring;
sentences.n: ὦ γύναι is ‘woman’, here a courteous address and not a curt one; the house rendering is kept. ἦ μάλα is ‘truly, very’, and ἔειπες the aorist ‘you have said’ with the epic doubled vowel. νημερτές ‘unerring’ agrees with ἔπος ‘word’, or may be taken as a neuter adverb, ‘unerringly’; either way the sense is that she has told the truth.

sentences.t:
ἤδη γὰρ καὶ δεῦρό ποτ’ ἤλυθε δῖος Ὀδυσσεὺς
σεῦ ἕνεκ’ ἀγγελίης σὺν ἀρηϊφίλῳ Μενελάῳ·
sentences.l:
For already once hither also came heavenly Odysseus
on an embassy for your sake, with Ares-loved Menelaus;
sentences.i: For heavenly Odysseus once came here before as well, on an embassy for your sake, with Menelaus, dear to Ares;
sentences.n: ἤδη … καὶ … ποτέ is ‘already once, too’, ἤλυθε the epic aorist of ἔρχομαι ‘came’, and δεῦρο ‘here’. δῖος ‘heavenly’ and ἀρηΐφιλος ‘Ares-loved’ (English ‘dear to Ares’) are stock epithets. σεῦ is the epic genitive of σύ, and σεῦ ἕνεκ’ ἀγγελίης is ‘for your sake, on an embassy’; ἀγγελίη is ‘message, news’ and is ‘news’ elsewhere in our English; here the thing carried is the errand itself, so ‘embassy’.

sentences.t:
τοὺς δ’ ἐγὼ ἐξείνισσα καὶ ἐν μεγάροισι φίλησα,
ἀμφοτέρων δὲ φυὴν ἐδάην καὶ μήδεα πυκνά.
sentences.l:
and them I entertained as guests and in my halls befriended,
and of both the stature I came to know, and the solid counsels.
sentences.i: I entertained them as my guests and treated them kindly in my halls, and I came to know the stature of both of them, and their solid counsels.
sentences.n: τούς … ἀμφοτέρων ‘them … of both’: ἐξείνισσα is the aorist of ξεινίζω ‘entertain as a guest’, ἐν μεγάροισι ‘in my halls’, and φίλησα the aorist of φιλέω ‘treat with love, befriend’. φυήν is ‘stature’ (what has grown, from φύω), and ἐδάην is the aorist passive form of δάω, ‘I learned, came to know’. μήδεα πυκνά ‘solid counsels’ recurs from 202, with the same English.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ Τρώεσσιν ἐν ἀγρομένοισιν ἔμιχθεν
στάντων μὲν Μενέλαος ὑπείρεχεν εὐρέας ὤμους,
ἄμφω δ’ ἑζομένω γεραρώτερος ἦεν Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.i: But when the two of them mingled with the Trojans gathered in assembly, then, as they stood, Menelaus rose above the other with his broad shoulders, but when both were seated, Odysseus was the more stately;
sentences.n: ἔμιχθεν is the aorist passive of μείγνυμι, ‘they mingled’, in the third person plural; ἀγρομένοισιν is the aorist middle participle of ἀγείρω ‘gather’, ‘assembled’. στάντων is the genitive plural of the aorist participle of ἵστημι, ‘of them standing’, set against ἄμφω ἑζομένω ‘both sitting’ (a dual participle of ἕζομαι); ὑπείρεχεν is the imperfect of ὑπερέχω ‘stand over, overtop’, with εὐρέας ὤμους ‘in broad shoulders’ an accusative of respect, and γεραρώτερος the comparative of γεραρός ‘stately’ (see 168). The meaning is that Menelaus stood the taller and Odysseus looked the nobler when seated.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ μύθους καὶ μήδεα πᾶσιν ὕφαινον
ἤτοι μὲν Μενέλαος ἐπιτροχάδην ἀγόρευε,
παῦρα μὲν ἀλλὰ μάλα λιγέως, ἐπεὶ οὐ πολύμυθος
οὐδ’ ἀφαμαρτοεπής·
sentences.l:
But when words and counsels for all they were weaving,
indeed then Menelaus spoke glibly,
few things, but very clearly, since he was not full of words
nor missing-the-mark in speech;
sentences.i: But when they were weaving words and counsels for all, Menelaus did speak glibly, a few things, but in a clear voice, since he was not talkative nor one who missed his mark in speech;
sentences.n: ὕφαινον is the imperfect of ὑφαίνω ‘weave’, a picture of speech-making as weaving (the Odyssey has the same image for plans and tricks, δόλον ὑφαίνειν ‘weave a trick’). ἤτοι (printed as one word) is ‘indeed’, and ἐπιτροχάδην ‘glibly’ is shipped in the Odyssey table (18.26) as ‘glibly’; παῦρα ‘few things’ and λιγέως ‘clearly’ (‘in a clear voice’) follow. πολύμυθος is ‘full of words’ (rendered ‘talkative’ in the English), and ἀφαμαρτοεπής is formed from ἀφαμαρτάνω ‘miss’ and ἔπος ‘word’, ‘missing the mark in speech’.

sentences.t: ἦ καὶ γένει ὕστερος ἦεν.
sentences.l: and indeed also in birth he was the younger.
sentences.i: and he was also the younger by birth.
sentences.n: ἦ καί is ‘and indeed’; γένει is the dative of respect ‘in birth’, and ὕστερος ‘later, younger’. ἦεν is the epic form of ἦν ‘was’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ πολύμητις ἀναΐξειεν Ὀδυσσεὺς
στάσκεν, ὑπαὶ δὲ ἴδεσκε κατὰ χθονὸς ὄμματα πήξας,
σκῆπτρον δ’ οὔτ’ ὀπίσω οὔτε προπρηνὲς ἐνώμα,
ἀλλ’ ἀστεμφὲς ἔχεσκεν ἀΐδρεϊ φωτὶ ἐοικώς·
sentences.l:
But whenever many-wiled Odysseus sprang up,
he would stand, and look down beneath with his eyes fixed on the ground,
and the sceptre neither backward nor forward he waved,
but stiff he would hold it, like a man who knew nothing;
sentences.i: But whenever Odysseus of many wiles sprang up, he would stand and look down, with his eyes fixed on the ground, and he would not wave the sceptre backward or forward, but hold it stiff, like a man who knew nothing;
sentences.n: ἀναΐξειεν is the aorist optative of ἀναΐσσω ‘spring up’, with ὅτε ‘whenever’, a general condition in the past, and the verbs that follow are iterative forms in -σκ-: στάσκεν ‘he would stand’, ἴδεσκε ‘he would look’, ἔχεσκεν ‘he would hold’. ὑπαί is ‘beneath, down’, and πήξας the aorist participle of πήγνυμι ‘fix’. ἐνώμα is the imperfect of νωμάω ‘wave, handle’; ὀπίσω ‘backward’ and προπρηνές ‘bending forward’. ἀστεμφές ‘stiff’ is the neuter adverb of ἀστεμφής, and ἀΐδρεϊ φωτί ‘a man without knowledge’ the dative with ἐοικώς ‘like’. The stock epithet πολύμητις is translated as in line 200.

sentences.t: φαίης κε ζάκοτόν τέ τιν’ ἔμμεναι ἄφρονά τ’ αὔτως.
sentences.l: you would say he was some greatly resentful man and simply senseless.
sentences.i: you would say he was some man full of resentment, and simply senseless.
sentences.n: φαίης κε is ‘you would say’, the optative with κε. ζάκοτον is ζα-, an intensifying prefix, with κότος ‘resentment’, so ‘greatly resentful’; ἄφρονα ‘senseless’ (without φρένες ‘wits’; the table’s ἄφρων), and αὔτως ‘simply, just so’. The sentence ends the picture of Odysseus before he speaks.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ ὄπα τε μεγάλην ἐκ στήθεος εἵη
καὶ ἔπεα νιφάδεσσιν ἐοικότα χειμερίῃσιν,
οὐκ ἂν ἔπειτ’ Ὀδυσῆΐ γ’ ἐρίσσειε βροτὸς ἄλλος·
sentences.i: But whenever he sent his great voice out from his chest, and words like wintry snowflakes, then no other mortal could rival Odysseus;
sentences.n: εἵη is the aorist optative of ἵημι ‘send forth’, with ὄπα (accusative of ὄψ ‘voice’) and ἔπεα ‘words’ as objects; ὅτε … εἵη is again ‘whenever’. νιφάδεσσιν χειμερίῃσιν is the epic dative plural of νιφάς ‘snowflake’ with ‘wintry’, after ἐοικότα ‘like’. οὐκ ἂν … ἐρίσσειε is the optative with ἄν, ‘would not rival’, with the dative Ὀδυσῆΐ.

sentences.t: οὐ τότε γ’ ὧδ’ Ὀδυσῆος ἀγασσάμεθ’ εἶδος ἰδόντες.
sentences.l: Not then so were we in wonder at Odysseus, having seen his form.”
sentences.i: we were not then so amazed at Odysseus when we saw his form.”
sentences.n: ἀγασσάμεθ’ is the aorist of ἀγάομαι, the verb of 181 (‘in wonder’ / ‘were amazed at’), here with the genitive Ὀδυσῆος. οὐ τότε γε ὧδε is ‘not then, so’: his looks did not amaze them as his voice did. εἶδος is ‘form’, and ἰδόντες the aorist participle ‘having seen’. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὸ τρίτον αὖτ’ Αἴαντα ἰδὼν ἐρέειν’ ὃ γεραιός·
sentences.l: Third, in turn, seeing Ajax, asked the old man:
sentences.i: Third, catching sight of Ajax, the old man asked:
sentences.n: τὸ τρίτον is ‘the third time’. ὃ (printed with a grave accent) is the article ὁ, ‘the old man’, as at 191.

sentences.t:
τίς τὰρ ὅδ’ ἄλλος Ἀχαιὸς ἀνὴρ ἠΰς τε μέγας τε
ἔξοχος Ἀργείων κεφαλήν τε καὶ εὐρέας ὤμους;
sentences.l:
“Who, then, is this other Achaean man, both good and great,
surpassing the Argives in head and broad shoulders?”
sentences.i: “Who then is this other Achaean, a man both good and great, who stands out above the Argives in head and broad shoulders?”
sentences.n: τίς τὰρ (the edition prints τὰρ as one word) is ‘who then?’, a lively question like τίς τ’ ἄρ at 1.8. ἠΰς … μέγας is ‘good and great’, as at 167. ἔξοχος is ‘standing out’, with the genitive Ἀργείων for those he excels; κεφαλήν and εὐρέας ὤμους are accusatives of respect, ‘in head and broad shoulders’. The question ends Priam’s speech.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ Ἑλένη τανύπεπλος ἀμείβετο δῖα γυναικῶν·
sentences.l: Him then Helen, long-robed, answered, heavenly-one of women:
sentences.i: Then long-robed Helen, heavenly among women, answered him:
sentences.n: The reply formula, as at 171, with the epithet τανύπεπλος ‘long-robed’ (τανύ- ‘long’ and πέπλος ‘robe’), fixed as Helen’s standing epithet at 4.305 of the Odyssey table. δῖα γυναικῶν is ‘heavenly-one of women’ as before.

sentences.t: οὗτος δ’ Αἴας ἐστὶ πελώριος ἕρκος Ἀχαιῶν·
sentences.l: “And this one is Ajax, huge, the fence of the Achaeans;
sentences.i: “This is huge Ajax, the bulwark of the Achaeans;
sentences.n: οὗτος δέ is ‘and this one’, picking out the man by name as at 178 and 200. πελώριος ‘huge’ is the adjective used of the man at 166. ἕρκος is a ‘fence, enclosure’, here the defence behind which the others stand, and has the same English as at 1.284 (‘fence’ in the literal layer, ‘bulwark’ in the English).

sentences.t:
Ἰδομενεὺς δ’ ἑτέρωθεν ἐνὶ Κρήτεσσι θεὸς ὣς
ἕστηκ’, ἀμφὶ δέ μιν Κρητῶν ἀγοὶ ἠγερέθονται.
sentences.l:
And Idomeneus, on the other side, among the Cretans, like a god,
stands, and around him the leaders of the Cretans are gathered.
sentences.i: On the other side Idomeneus stands among the Cretans like a god, and the Cretan leaders are gathered around him.
sentences.n: ἑτέρωθεν is ‘from the other side, on the other side’. θεὸς ὣς is ‘like a god’, and ἕστηκ’ is ἕστηκε, the perfect of ἵστημι, which has the sense of the present ‘stands’. ἀμφί … ἠγερέθονται is ‘are gathered around’ (the verb ἠγερέθομαι is a poetic form of ἀγείρομαι), with μιν ‘him’; ἀγοί are ‘leaders’, from ἄγω ‘lead’.

sentences.t:
πολλάκι μιν ξείνισσεν ἀρηΐφιλος Μενέλαος
οἴκῳ ἐν ἡμετέρῳ ὁπότε Κρήτηθεν ἵκοιτο.
sentences.l:
Often him entertained as a guest Ares-loved Menelaus
in our house, whenever from Crete he came.
sentences.i: Menelaus, dear to Ares, often entertained him as a guest in our house, whenever he came from Crete.
sentences.n: ξείνισσεν is the imperfect of ξεινίζω ‘entertain as a guest’ (without the augment), with ἀρηΐφιλος Μενέλαος ‘Menelaus, dear to Ares’ as its subject. ἡμετέρῳ is ‘our’, so Helen was in the house. ὁπότε … ἵκοιτο is ‘whenever he came’, the optative of a repeated action in the past, and Κρήτηθεν ‘from Crete’ has the suffix -θεν ‘from’.

sentences.t:
νῦν δ’ ἄλλους μὲν πάντας ὁρῶ ἑλίκωπας Ἀχαιούς,
οὕς κεν ἐῢ γνοίην καί τ’ οὔνομα μυθησαίμην·
sentences.l:
And now all the others I see, the quick-eyed Achaeans,
whom I could well recognise and could tell the name of;
sentences.i: Now I see all the other quick-eyed Achaeans, whom I could recognise well and whose names I could tell;
sentences.n: νῦν δέ sets the present against the past of 232–233; ἄλλους … πάντας is ‘all the others’, and ἑλίκωπας Ἀχαιούς ‘the quick-eyed Achaeans’, as at 190. οὕς κεν … γνοίην is the optative with κεν, ‘whom I could recognise’, with ἐΰ ‘well’; καί τ’ is ‘and also’, and μυθησαίμην is the aorist optative of μυθέομαι, ‘I could tell, speak’, with οὔνομα ‘name’ as its object.

sentences.t:
δοιὼ δ’ οὐ δύναμαι ἰδέειν κοσμήτορε λαῶν
Κάστορά θ’ ἱππόδαμον καὶ πὺξ ἀγαθὸν Πολυδεύκεα
αὐτοκασιγνήτω, τώ μοι μία γείνατο μήτηρ.
sentences.l:
But two I cannot see, the two marshallers of the people,
Castor, horse-taming, and Polydeuces, good with the fist,
own brothers, the two whom one mother bore to me.
sentences.i: But there are two I cannot see, the two marshals of the people, Castor, tamer of horses, and Polydeuces, good with his fists, my own brothers, whom one mother bore for me.
sentences.n: δοιώ is ‘two’, and κοσμήτορε the dual of κοσμήτωρ ‘marshal’, as at 1.16; ἰδέειν is the aorist infinitive of ‘see’. Line 237 is a line of the Odyssey (11.300), with the same English: ἱππόδαμος ‘horse-taming’ (‘tamer of horses’) and πὺξ ἀγαθός ‘good with the fist’. αὐτοκασιγνήτω is the dual ‘own brothers’, and τώ the dual relative ‘whom (two)’, with μοι ‘for me’ and γείνατο the aorist middle of γείνομαι ‘bear’.

sentences.t:
ἢ οὐχ ἑσπέσθην Λακεδαίμονος ἐξ ἐρατεινῆς,
ἢ δεύρω μὲν ἕποντο νέεσσ’ ἔνι ποντοπόροισι,
νῦν αὖτ’ οὐκ ἐθέλουσι μάχην καταδύμεναι ἀνδρῶν
αἴσχεα δειδιότες καὶ ὀνείδεα πόλλ’ ἅ μοί ἐστιν.
sentences.l:
Either they did not follow from Lacedaemon, the lovely,
or hither they did follow in sea-crossing ships,
but now again are unwilling to enter the fighting of men,
dreading the shames and the many reproaches that are mine.”
sentences.i: Either they did not follow from lovely Lacedaemon, or they followed here in their sea-crossing ships and now again are unwilling to enter the fighting of men, dreading the shames and the many reproaches that are mine.”
sentences.n: ἑσπέσθην is the aorist dual of ἕπομαι ‘follow’; ἢ … ἢ is ‘either … or’, and ἕποντο the imperfect plural, ‘they followed’. ἐρατεινῆς ‘lovely’, and ποντοπόροισι ‘sea-crossing’ is the epithet of ships; ἔνι is ἐν placed after its noun. νῦν αὖτ’ is ‘but now again’, καταδύμεναι the infinitive of καταδύω ‘go down into, enter’, with μάχην ἀνδρῶν ‘the fighting of men’. δειδιότες is the perfect participle of δείδω ‘dread’, αἴσχεα ‘shames’ and ὀνείδεα ‘reproaches’ are its objects, and ἅ μοί ἐστιν ‘which are mine’ says that the reproaches are Helen’s own, which her brothers dread to share. The speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο, τοὺς δ’ ἤδη κάτεχεν φυσίζοος αἶα
ἐν Λακεδαίμονι αὖθι φίλῃ ἐν πατρίδι γαίῃ.
sentences.l:
So she spoke; but them already the life-giving earth held fast
in Lacedaemon, there, in the dear land of their fathers.
sentences.i: So she spoke; but the life-giving earth already held them fast, there in Lacedaemon, in the dear land of their fathers.
sentences.n: ὣς φάτο is the closing formula ‘so she spoke’. The narrator now tells what Helen does not know: τοὺς … κάτεχεν, ‘held them fast’, is the imperfect of κατέχω, with the stock epithet φυσίζοος αἶα ‘the life-giving earth’, rendered the same way every time. αὖθι is ‘right there’, and πατρίδι is the adjective ‘of the fathers’, agreeing with γαίῃ ‘land’, so ‘in the dear land of their fathers’.

sentences.t:
κήρυκες δ’ ἀνὰ ἄστυ θεῶν φέρον ὅρκια πιστὰ
ἄρνε δύω καὶ οἶνον ἐΰφρονα καρπὸν ἀρούρης
ἀσκῷ ἐν αἰγείῳ·
sentences.i: Meanwhile heralds were carrying through the city the faithful oaths of the gods: two lambs, and heart-cheering wine, the fruit of the plough-land, in a goatskin;
sentences.n: κήρυκες ‘heralds’ are the subject, φέρον the imperfect ‘were bringing’, and ἀνὰ ἄστυ ‘up and down the city’. ὅρκια πιστά ‘faithful oaths’ is the house rendering, but here the word names the things that make the oath, which the next lines list: ἄρνε δύω ‘two lambs’ (the dual), οἶνον ‘wine’ and ἀσκῷ αἰγείῳ ‘in a goatskin’. ἐΰφρονα is ‘kindly, gladdening’ (εὖ ‘well’ and φρήν ‘mind’), here said of the wine, ‘heart-cheering’, and καρπὸν ἀρούρης ‘fruit of the plough-land’ is the vine’s.

sentences.t:
φέρε δὲ κρητῆρα φαεινὸν
κῆρυξ Ἰδαῖος ἠδὲ χρύσεια κύπελλα·
sentences.l:
and carried a mixing-bowl, shining,
the herald Idaeus, and golden cups;
sentences.i: and the herald Idaeus carried a shining mixing-bowl and golden cups;
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of the line. φέρε is the imperfect of φέρω ‘carry’ (without the augment), κρητῆρα φαεινόν ‘a shining mixing-bowl’ the vessel in which wine and water are mixed, and Ἰδαῖος the herald Idaeus. χρύσεια κύπελλα are ‘golden cups’, joined by ἠδέ ‘and’.

sentences.t: ὄτρυνεν δὲ γέροντα παριστάμενος ἐπέεσσιν·
sentences.l: and he urged on the old man, standing beside him, with words:
sentences.i: and, standing beside the old man, he urged him on with words:
sentences.n: The subject is Idaeus. ὄτρυνεν is the imperfect (without the augment) of ὀτρύνω ‘urge on’, γέροντα ‘old man’ is Priam, παριστάμενος is ‘standing beside’, and ἐπέεσσιν the epic dative plural of ἔπος ‘word’.

sentences.t:
ὄρσεο Λαομεδοντιάδη, καλέουσιν ἄριστοι
Τρώων θ’ ἱπποδάμων καὶ Ἀχαιῶν χαλκοχιτώνων
ἐς πεδίον καταβῆναι ἵν’ ὅρκια πιστὰ τάμητε·
sentences.i: “Rise, son of Laomedon: the best of the Trojans, tamers of horses, and of the bronze-shirted Achaeans are calling you to go down to the plain, so that you may swear faithful oaths;
sentences.n: ὄρσεο is the aorist middle imperative of ὄρνυμι, ‘rouse yourself, rise’, and Λαομεδοντιάδη the vocative of the patronymic ‘son of Laomedon’, Priam. καλέουσιν ἄριστοι is ‘the best are calling’. Line 251 is line 127 again, with the same English. ἐς πεδίον καταβῆναι is ‘to go down to the plain’ (the aorist infinitive of καταβαίνω), and ἵν’ … τάμητε the aorist subjunctive of τάμνω ‘cut’ (second person plural, for the two kings): oaths are ‘cut’ because victims are cut in swearing them.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ἀλέξανδρος καὶ ἀρηΐφιλος Μενέλαος
μακρῇς ἐγχείῃσι μαχήσοντ’ ἀμφὶ γυναικί·
sentences.l:
but Alexander and Ares-loved Menelaus
with long spears will fight about a woman;
sentences.i: but Alexander and Menelaus, dear to Ares, will fight with their long spears for a woman;
sentences.n: The first line is 136 again, with the same English up to the verb. μακρῇς ἐγχείῃσι is the epic dative plural ‘with long spears’, μαχήσοντ’ is μαχήσονται, the future of μάχομαι ‘fight’, and ἀμφὶ γυναικί ‘about a woman’, with the dative of ἀμφί, names the stake: Helen is the prize.

sentences.t: τῷ δέ κε νικήσαντι γυνὴ καὶ κτήμαθ’ ἕποιτο·
sentences.l: and with the one who wins, the woman and the possessions would go;
sentences.i: and the woman and the possessions would follow whichever of them wins;
sentences.n: τῷ … νικήσαντι is the dative of the aorist participle, ‘for the one who has won’, and ἕποιτο the optative of ἕπομαι ‘follow’ with κε, ‘would follow’: the stated result of the duel. κτήμαθ’ is κτήματα ‘possessions’, as at 72.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ἄλλοι φιλότητα καὶ ὅρκια πιστὰ ταμόντες
ναίοιμεν Τροίην ἐριβώλακα, τοὶ δὲ νέονται
Ἄργος ἐς ἱππόβοτον καὶ Ἀχαιΐδα καλλιγύναικα.
sentences.l:
and we others, friendship and faithful oaths having cut,
may we dwell in rich-soiled Troy, and they are going back
to Argos horse-pasturing and Achaea of the fair women.”
sentences.i: and the rest of us, having made friendship and sworn faithful oaths, may we live in rich-soiled Troy, while they go back to horse-pasturing Argos and to Achaea of the fair women.”
sentences.n: These lines closely repeat 73–75, with two changes: ναίοιμεν is the first-person optative, ‘may we dwell’, since the speaker counts himself among the Trojans, and νέονται is the present ‘they are going back’, in place of the imperative νεέσθων of 74. οἳ δ’ ἄλλοι is ‘and we others’; φιλότητα καὶ ὅρκια πιστὰ ταμόντες is ‘having cut friendship and faithful oaths’; ἐριβώλακα ‘rich-soiled’, ἱππόβοτον ‘horse-pasturing’ and καλλιγύναικα ‘of the fair women’ are stock epithets, translated as in the earlier lines. The speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο ῥίγησεν δ’ ὃ γέρων, ἐκέλευσε δ’ ἑταίρους
ἵππους ζευγνύμεναι·
sentences.l:
So he spoke; and shuddered the old man, and he bade his companions
yoke the horses;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and the old man shuddered and told his companions to yoke the horses;
sentences.n: ὣς φάτο is the closing formula. ῥίγησεν is the aorist of ῥιγέω ‘shudder’, and ὃ γέρων ‘the old man’ is Priam (the Greek says nothing more than that he shuddered; the reader is left to find the reason in the duel). ἐκέλευσε is ‘bade’ with the accusative ἑταίρους ‘companions’, and ζευγνύμεναι is the infinitive of ζεύγνυμι ‘yoke’, ‘to yoke’. The unit ends in the middle of the line.

sentences.t: τοὶ δ’ ὀτραλέως ἐπίθοντο.
sentences.l: and they promptly obeyed.
sentences.i: and they obeyed promptly.
sentences.n: τοί is the article used as ‘they’, ὀτραλέως ‘promptly’, and ἐπίθοντο the aorist middle of πείθομαι ‘obey’. The unit begins in the middle of the line.

sentences.t: ἂν δ’ ἄρ’ ἔβη Πρίαμος, κατὰ δ’ ἡνία τεῖνεν ὀπίσσω·
sentences.l: And up went Priam, and the reins he drew tight backward;
sentences.i: Priam mounted, and drew the reins back tight;
sentences.n: ἂν … ἔβη is ἀνέβη ‘went up’ (onto the chariot) with the preposition ἀνά split from its verb (tmesis), and κατὰ … τεῖνεν is likewise the imperfect of κατατείνω ‘draw tight’, without the augment. ἡνία ‘reins’ is the object; ὀπίσσω is ‘backward, back’.

sentences.t: πὰρ δέ οἱ Ἀντήνωρ περικαλλέα βήσετο δίφρον·
sentences.l: and beside him Antenor the very beautiful chariot mounted;
sentences.i: and beside him Antenor stepped up into the very beautiful chariot;
sentences.n: πὰρ is παρά ‘beside’, with οἱ ‘him’ (Priam). περικαλλέα is ‘very beautiful’ (περί ‘exceedingly’ with κάλλος ‘beauty’), agreeing with δίφρον ‘chariot’, and βήσετο is the epic aorist middle of βαίνω ‘mount’.

sentences.t: τὼ δὲ διὰ Σκαιῶν πεδίον δ’ ἔχον ὠκέας ἵππους.
sentences.l: and the two through the Scaean gates to the plain held the swift horses.
sentences.i: and the two drove the swift horses through the Scaean Gates toward the plain.
sentences.n: τὼ is the dual article ‘the two’, Priam and Antenor. Σκαιῶν is the genitive plural of Σκαιαί, the Scaean Gates (πύλαι ‘gates’ is understood), after διά ‘through’; πεδίον δ’ is πεδίονδε ‘to the plain’, with the -δε of direction. ἔχον is the imperfect of ἔχω ‘hold, keep’, with ἵππους as its object, ‘held the horses on their way’, so ‘drove’; ὠκέας ‘swift’ is the epic accusative plural of ὠκύς. The part ends with the chariot moving out of the city.
